analysis.one_liner: Requires every state to draw its congressional map with an independent commission and bans mid-decade redistricting.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee from May 2023 until the Congress ended in January 2025, with no other member of the House signing on and no vote ever scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would take the drawing of congressional district lines out of the hands of state legislators and give it to an independent commission in each state, with strict rules against favoring a party or protecting an incumbent. It would also ban a state from redrawing its congressional map more than once per decade unless a court orders it, and would send federal money to states to pay for the commissions. The changes would only apply after the 2030 census.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters in every state with more than one congressional district. District lines would be drawn by a citizen commission barred from considering party affiliation, voting history, or where incumbents live, and states could no longer redraw maps mid-decade to lock in a partisan advantage.

how_it_helps.text: Each state must create an independent redistricting commission whose members cannot have held office, run for office, or worked for a party or candidate in the previous four years, and who must pledge not to run for Congress until after the next census.

The commission is barred from considering voters' party affiliation, past voting behavior, or the home addresses of sitting House members when drawing districts, except where needed to comply with the Voting Rights Act.

A state may not be redistricted again after its once-per-decade map unless a court orders it to comply with the Constitution or the Voting Rights Act, which would stop mid-decade remaps pursued for partisan gain.
Commission meetings must be public, states must run a website with precinct-level data and interactive mapping software, and the public can submit its own proposed maps and comments.
If a commission's plan is not enacted, the state's highest court or a federal district court must adopt or draw a plan under the same standards, so the process cannot simply stall.

analysis.who_pays: The party that controls a state legislature, and the members of Congress whose seats depend on the lines those legislators draw. Incumbents lose the ability to tailor their own districts, and legislative majorities lose the power to engineer safe seats. Federal taxpayers fund the commissions at $150,000 per congressional seat.

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides state constitutional procedures for redistricting: a state legislature could only approve or reject a commission plan without amendment, and courts would draw maps whenever a commission's plan fails to become law, which shifts power away from state governments.

The commission design still routes appointments through the leaders of the two major parties in each chamber of the state legislature, so partisans choose the supposedly independent members in most states.
It applies only to redistricting after the 2030 census, so it would change nothing about the maps in force through the end of this decade.
Federal payments of $150,000 per congressional seat, with no dollar cap on total appropriations, add new federal spending for a process states have historically funded themselves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: voters get district lines drawn by people barred from serving their own party's advantage, at the cost of $150,000 in federal money per seat and a real transfer of power from state legislatures to commissions and courts. The appointment design has a genuine weakness — party leaders in the legislature still pick the members — but the ban on mid-decade remaps and the prohibition on considering incumbents' homes and voters' party affiliation target the main tools legislators use to make their own seats safe. On balance the public benefit outweighs the costs, though the bill's failure to attract a single cosponsor suggests no realistic path to passing it in its current form.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and the two-year Congress ended with no vote ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Representative Steve Cohen of Tennessee introduced the bill on May 11, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor, leaving the bill with a single sponsor for its entire two-year run.
The bill received no further action after the committee referral; it was never reported out of committee, never debated, and never voted on in either chamber.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died with it, without any version of the redistricting changes moving forward.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent House members and the legislative majorities that draw state maps kept their control over district lines, including the ability to remap mid-decade, since no change ever reached the floor. The bill's sponsor, a lone member without cosponsors, also bears some responsibility for not building support before the Congress closed.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee; named it for two former Tennessee representatives, John Tanner and Jim Cooper.

against.name: Rep. Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to; the committee never held a markup or reported the bill out during the two-year Congress.

against.name: House leadership of the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote, and no suspension or rule vote on it appears in the action history.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsor ever joined, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never tested — the bill's sponsor was a Democrat and the committee and House majority that buried it were Republican.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislative majorities
industries.note: The bill strips map-drawing power from the politicians it affects: commissions are barred from considering incumbents' residences or voters' party affiliation, and mid-decade remaps are banned except by court order. Legislators who currently draw their own districts and their parties' safe seats lose that power entirely.

Party leaders in each state legislature still appoint the commission members, giving the two major parties continued influence over who draws the lines, but they lose the final say over the maps themselves and cannot consider party affiliation in drawing them.
